passage:
Diary, 2 a.m.
Can't sleep again. It's not one thing, it's everything. The heat this summer, the floods on the news, board exams, whether I'll get into a college, whether there'll even be jobs. And then I wonder where I even fit in all this. I'm one person who can't even finish her chemistry. Ira texted earlier, "Mehak u ok? u were quiet today." I said "just tired." I wasn't. I'm going to tell her tomorrow, properly. Maybe Mum too. It helped a bit just writing this down. The fan is squeaking. At least that's something I understand.

qa.q: What did Ira text Mehak?
qa.a: "Mehak u ok? u were quiet today."

qa.q: What is Mehak feeling at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: A heavy, spread-out dread about the world and her future, and unsure where she fits in it all.

qa.q: What small steps is Mehak already taking, and why do they help?
qa.a: Writing it down and planning to tell Ira and her mum properly, because sharing the worry makes it less lonely.

qa.q: How might Ira feel if Mehak tells her the truth tomorrow?
qa.a: Probably relieved she asked, and glad to be trusted with more than "just tired." 🤍

grounding: It shows a teenager's sleepless, general dread about the world and her place in it, and her first steps to share it.

passage: Every evening Baljeet, seventeen, sat with Dhruv on the canal bridge outside their village, watching the water sit lower each year. Half the boys from their class had already filled in forms to go abroad. The fields their fathers ploughed felt smaller somehow, and the news on the radio only ever seemed to get worse. "What are we even going to do here?" Baljeet asked, throwing a pebble. "Or anywhere?" Dhruv shrugged. Baljeet felt a tight, restless anger with no one to point it at. At home he snapped at his little sister for nothing, then sat on the roof until late. The next morning he asked his teacher, Masterji, if they could talk after school. "I don't know what's wrong," he said. "Everything, I think."

qa.q: Where did Baljeet and Dhruv sit every evening?
qa.a: On the canal bridge outside their village.

qa.q: What was the "tight, restless anger" Baljeet felt about?
qa.a: Not one thing, but his uncertain future, friends leaving and a world that seemed to get worse, with no one to blame.

qa.q: Why is talking to Masterji a good step?
qa.a: A trusted adult can listen and help him sort the big, vague dread into smaller things he can face.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's little sister have experienced his snapping?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since she did nothing wrong and cannot see the worry behind it.

grounding: It shows a village teenager's generalised frustration and dread about his future and place in the world.

passage: On the bus home through São Paulo traffic, Priscila, sixteen, watched the brown haze sit over the towers and felt the familiar tightness start. Geography class had been about rising seas again. She did the maths in her head: in thirty years she'd be forty-six. Would there be jobs? Would the coast still be there? What was the point of studying for exams about a world that might be falling apart? At home she lay on the floor with her earphones in and no music playing. Her brother Felix, twelve, stepped over her. 'You're doing the floor thing again.' 'Everything's broken, Felix.' He considered this, then lay down beside her. 'Is dinner broken? Mãe made feijoada.' She laughed despite herself and sat up.

qa.q: What had geography class been about?
qa.a: Rising seas.

qa.q: What does Priscila lying on the floor with no music playing suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt weighed down and withdrawn, overwhelmed by worry about the future.

qa.q: How could a parent or teacher support Priscila with these feelings?
qa.a: They could listen without dismissing her worries, help her find one small real action, and involve a counsellor if the dread keeps growing.

qa.q: How does Felix seem to see his sister's 'floor thing'?
qa.a: He is used to it and doesn't argue; he joins her and uses humour to pull her back to something ordinary.

grounding: Shows a teenager's diffuse dread about the world's future and her place in it, eased a little by her brother.

passage: The school library was meant to be silent, but Seema kept clicking her pen. 'Did you see the pictures from the floods up north? And fees going up again, and my brother still without a job after his degree.' Himani, beside her, closed her book. 'You've been like this all week.' 'Because it's all the same thing. Adults broke everything and we're supposed to fix it by writing essays about the monsoon.' Her voice rose; the librarian looked over. Seema pressed her forehead to the cool table. 'I'm not even sad. I'm just angry at nothing and everything.' Himani slid a note across: 'Walk after this period? The counsellor's door is open on Thursdays too.' Seema read it twice and nodded without lifting her head.

qa.q: What was Seema clicking in the library?
qa.a: Her pen.

qa.q: What did Seema mean by 'angry at nothing and everything'?
qa.a: She feels a broad, heavy frustration about the world and her future that does not point at one clear thing.

qa.q: What makes Himani's note a helpful response?
qa.a: It offers a simple next step and mentions the counsellor without lecturing or embarrassing Seema in the library.

qa.q: How might the librarian have seen Seema's raised voice?
qa.a: She may have seen only a noisy student, without knowing the worry underneath.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's general frustration and dread about the world, and a friend responding with care.

passage:
Dear Tenzin,
I know you're busy with college, but I need to tell someone. Lately I feel this weight all the time. I read the news and it's floods, jobs disappearing, prices going up. Then I think about board exams, and whether any of it even matters. I'm not sad exactly. More like angry and scared at the same time, and I can't point to one reason. At night my head won't stop. I told Amma yesterday and she said we'll go and see the school counsellor together on Monday. I'm glad I said it out loud. Can you call this weekend? You always make things feel smaller.
Irawati

qa.q: When will Irawati and Amma see the school counsellor?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: How would you describe what Irawati is feeling?
qa.a: Irawati feels anxious, angry and scared about the world and the future, without one clear reason.

qa.q: What did Irawati do well, and what else could help?
qa.a: Irawati told Amma and agreed to see the counsellor; talking to Tenzin and taking breaks from the news could also help.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Concerned for Irawati, and glad Irawati reached out and told Amma.

grounding: Shows a teenager's generalised dread and frustration about the world and one's place in it, and reaching out for support.

passage: Imran, you asked why I've been so short with everyone. You know me, Anirban, the one who always had a plan? Lately I don't. Every time I open my phone it's layoffs, heatwaves, some war. My father says study hard and you'll be fine, but his office just cut half the staff. I lie awake angry at everyone and scared of nothing I can name. I snapped at my sister for breathing too loudly. That's not me. Last week I told our class teacher, and she set up a meeting with the school counsellor for Thursday. I don't expect a magic fix. I just didn't want to carry this alone any more, so I'm telling you too.

qa.q: When is Anirban's meeting with the school counsellor?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What is Anirban feeling while lying awake at night?
qa.a: Anirban feels angry and scared at once, a general dread about the future with no single cause.

qa.q: What was a good step in Anirban's story, and what else could help?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher and a friend; cutting down late-night news on the phone could also help.

qa.q: How might Imran feel hearing all this?
qa.a: Concerned, but also trusted and glad that Anirban chose to share it.

grounding: Shows a teenager's generalised anger and dread about the world and the future, and a decision to seek support.

passage: I'm Anand, Sharmila's younger brother. This term Sharmila, who's sixteen, stays up late reading the news on her phone, and in the mornings she's snappy and tired. Last night at dinner she pushed her plate away and said, "Why study if the whole world is falling apart?" Nobody knew what to say. Amma followed her to her room and sat on the bed with her for a long time. Later Amma told us they'd agreed on no phone after ten and a visit to the school counsellor this week. This morning Sharmila put her phone on the kitchen shelf before bed. I don't know what's inside her head, but she looked a little lighter.

qa.q: What did Sharmila say at dinner?
qa.a: "Why study if the whole world is falling apart?"

qa.q: What might Sharmila be feeling when she pushes her plate away?
qa.a: She seems anxious and frustrated, weighed down by a general dread about the world.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Sharmila, listened, and agreed on small steps: no phone after ten and a visit to the school counsellor.

qa.q: How does Anand see the change in Sharmila?
qa.a: He notices she looks a little lighter, though he admits he can't know what's inside her head.

grounding: Shows a teenager's dread about the world and her place in it, noticed by her brother, and the family's supportive response.

passage:
Monday: Vijay, sixteen, scrolled news about floods, heatwaves and job losses until two in the morning. He couldn't sleep. What was the point of studying for a future that might not exist? He felt tight and irritated all day.
Thursday: His aunt Ganga noticed him snapping at everyone. On the terrace, he told her how scared he was about everything at once. She didn't laugh. "I feel it too sometimes," she said. "Can we cut the late-night news, and do one small thing?"
Two weeks later: Vijay was digging holes with the colony's tree-planting group on a Sunday morning, mud on his shorts. He still worried. But he slept better, and it felt good to do something with his hands.

qa.q: Who did Vijay talk to on the terrace?
qa.a: His aunt Ganga.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after scrolling the news until two in the morning?
qa.a: He felt anxious, tense and irritated, full of dread about the future.

qa.q: What small steps helped Vijay cope with his worries?
qa.a: Cutting late-night news and joining the tree-planting group, so he felt less alone and more able to act.

qa.q: How did Ganga see Vijay's worries?
qa.a: She took them seriously, sharing that she felt the same sometimes.

grounding: Over two weeks, a teenager moves from late-night dread about the world to coping with his aunt's support.

passage: Leela Nani put her knitting down. "Nirmala, when I was fifteen, there was a drought three years in a row. The well in our town went dry. Every night I lay awake thinking, what if it never rains again? What if we have to leave? What am I even studying for? I was angry at everyone. My teacher, Mrs Pinto, noticed I'd stopped answering in class. She kept me back one day and asked me what was wrong. I told her everything. She said, 'Worry is a sign you care. Let's give that caring a job.' She made me the school water monitor. Counting buckets. It sounds silly. But having something to do made the fear smaller." Nirmala looked at her phone, full of news. "Did it ever go away?" "Not fully. But I learned to carry it."

qa.q: What did Mrs Pinto make young Leela?
qa.a: The school water monitor.

qa.q: How did young Leela feel during the drought years?
qa.a: She felt anxious, angry and full of dread about the future.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Leela's story?
qa.a: Mrs Pinto keeping her back to ask what was wrong, then giving her a job that turned her worry into action.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pinto have seen young Leela when she stopped answering in class?
qa.a: She likely felt concerned that something was troubling Leela and wanted to help.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, as a teenager, she felt dread during a drought and learned to cope with a teacher's help.

passage: The night before board results, the power went off in the Ranchi flat. The heat pressed down. Ojas, seventeen, sat on the balcony in the dark, his phone at five percent. "What's even the point of all this studying," he muttered. "Marks, college, then what? Everyone's stressed. The world's on fire." His sister Bhavna came out with two glasses of water. She sat beside him. "Say more." He did: the results, the news, the feeling that nothing he did would change anything out there. She listened. "That's a lot to carry at midnight." "It is." "Tomorrow, after results, whatever they are, will you talk to the school counsellor with me? I went last year." Ojas nodded slowly. "Okay." They sat together until the fan came back on.

qa.q: What percentage was Ojas's phone at?
qa.a: Five percent.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he muttered "What's even the point"?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed, frustrated and full of dread about the results and the world.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with him, listened without arguing, and offered to go with him to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt hearing her brother talk like this?
qa.a: She may have felt worried but calm, wanting him to feel less alone.

grounding: During a power cut before results, a teenager voices a sense of dread and his sister supports him.

passage:
Shankar stood on the metro platform in Delhi at 7 a.m. with his earphones in but nothing playing. The news on the screen showed floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.
He'd been like this for weeks. Not sad, exactly. More like the air had weight. What was the point of board exams if the planet was cooking? What was he even supposed to become in a world like this?
His friend Yash came up behind him and tugged an earphone out. "You look like you're carrying the whole city."
Shankar shrugged. "Maybe I am."
Yash didn't laugh. "Me too, some days. Want to walk from the next station? The long way?"
They walked. It didn't fix anything, but the air felt lighter.

qa.q: What did the news screen show?
qa.a: Floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling on the platform?
qa.a: He felt a heavy, generalised dread and frustration, as if the air had weight and nothing had a point.

qa.q: How could an adult support Shankar if this feeling keeps going?
qa.a: A parent or school counsellor could listen without dismissing his worries and help him find small things he can do and enjoy.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash when he sees Shankar that morning?
qa.a: Yash recognises the feeling because he has it too, so he responds with company rather than a joke.

grounding: Shows a teen carrying diffuse dread about the world and a friend's quiet support.

passage:
"Why are you still awake?" Anirban whispered from the top bunk.
Vinita didn't answer for a while. "Do you ever think we're too late for everything?"
"Too late for what?"
"For good jobs. For clean air. For anything to be normal. Everyone keeps saying study hard and you'll be fine. I don't believe them."
"That's a lot for midnight, didi."
"I know." She pulled the blanket up. "It's just there. All the time. Like background noise."
Anirban climbed down and sat on the edge of her bunk. "I don't know the answers. But you're not the only one. Half my class says the same."
"Really?"
"Really. Tell Maa tomorrow? She keeps asking why you're so quiet."
Vinita nodded in the dark. "Tomorrow."

qa.q: What does Vinita say the feeling is like?
qa.a: Like background noise, there all the time.

qa.q: How is Vinita feeling as she talks in the dark?
qa.a: She feels anxious and hopeless about the future, not believing that studying hard will make things fine.

qa.q: What small step does Anirban suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: He suggests telling Maa tomorrow, since sharing the worry with a trusted adult can ease it and bring support.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel hearing his older sister say this at midnight?
qa.a: He may feel worried and a bit out of his depth, but caring enough to climb down and sit beside her.

grounding: Shows a teen voicing generalised dread about the future to a younger sibling.

passage:
Last term I kept a list on my phone called "Why bother." I'm Vikas, and I'm a bit embarrassed by it now.
Every night I'd add something: the heat wave, the job cuts on the news, a video of melting ice. I'd lie there scrolling until two. In the morning I'd be too tired to care about school, then angry at myself for not caring.
My friend Devika noticed during a free period. "You look like someone switched you off," she said. I showed her the list. She didn't tell me to cheer up. She said, "Now write one you can do."
I wrote: plant the balcony tulsi again. Help at the Saturday clean-up. Sleep before twelve.
The dread didn't vanish. But I have two lists now, and the second one is longer.

qa.q: What was the name of the list on Vikas's phone?
qa.a: "Why bother."

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel when she saw Vikas in the free period?
qa.a: She seemed concerned, noticing Vikas looked switched off, and caring enough to respond without brushing it off.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas if the dread comes back strongly?
qa.a: Keep using the second list and talk to a trusted adult or school counsellor if it keeps going or worries Vikas.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had told Vikas to cheer up?
qa.a: Vikas might have felt dismissed and kept scrolling, instead of finding small things to do.

grounding: A teen recalls a spell of dread about the world and a friend's practical nudge.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
Lalremsiami came in at lunch with her friend Shreya, who said, "She hasn't been sleeping." Lalremsiami said she keeps reading about floods and heatwaves at night and wonders why she should plan for college "when everything might be underwater by then." She said it angrily, then went quiet and pressed her palms into her eyes. She also said she's scared she'll never be good enough to fix anything. I didn't argue with her fears. I listened, said it sounds heavy to carry, and asked what small thing feels in her control. She mentioned the school garden club. We agreed she'll try one session, keep news reading out of bedtime, and meet me again Monday. With her agreement, I'm calling her mother today.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami keep reading about at night?
qa.a: Floods and heatwaves.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she pressed her palms into her eyes?
qa.a: She seemed overwhelmed, a mix of anger, fear and dread about the future and her place in it.

qa.q: What did the counsellor's approach get right?
qa.a: The counsellor listened without arguing, named how heavy it felt, found one small step in her control, and arranged follow-up and support at home.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya to bring Lalremsiami in?
qa.a: Shreya is clearly worried about a friend who isn't sleeping and cares enough to walk Lalremsiami to the counsellor.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's general dread and frustration about the world's future and a counsellor's calm response.
